vignette:
Marcus is a thirty-seven-year-old financial analyst who was divorced two years ago, and he came to see me after his primary care physician referred him following a routine checkup where he disclosed that he had been struggling to sleep, that he felt constantly on edge, and that he had been avoiding his own living room for months. He sat at the edge of the chair, his hands folded tightly in his lap, and told me that he needed to understand why he could not seem to move forward from something that had happened four years earlier, during a business trip to a country he had never wanted to visit in the first place.

The event itself lasted six days. Marcus had been part of a small team sent to finalize an acquisition, and on the second evening, their hotel was raided by a local militia group that had been extorting foreign companies for years. He and two colleagues were taken to a windowless concrete room in a compound on the outskirts of the city. They were held there, blindfolded for most of the time, while armed men came and went. What Marcus remembered most vividly now, what he could still smell if he let his mind drift, was the odor of diesel fuel mixed with sweat and the metallic tang of blood from a guard who had been injured before they arrived. That smell would hit him without warning—sometimes when he walked past a gas station, sometimes when he opened a new bottle of cleaning fluid—and suddenly he would be back in that room, his wrists raw from the zip ties, the silence pressing in on him between interrogations. That silence was the worst part, he said. When the men left and the room went completely quiet, he could hear his own heartbeat and the shallow breathing of his colleagues, and he was certain that the quiet meant they were about to be killed. Now, silence in his own apartment did the same thing. He had started keeping the television on at all times, even when he was not watching it, because the sudden hush of an empty room made his chest tighten and his palms sweat.

He was released after a ransom was paid, and he returned to the United States feeling hollowed out. For the first few months, he told almost no one what had happened. He went back to work, but he found himself unable to concentrate in the open-plan office, where the murmur of conversations and the clatter of keyboards felt like a constant low-grade threat. He requested permission to work from home, and his manager agreed. That was when the pattern solidified. At home, he found that he could not relax. He was hypervigilant even in his own kitchen, checking the locks on the front door three or four times before he could sit down to eat. He slept poorly because he felt he had to stay alert—he would lie in bed, listening for footsteps, for the sound of a door being forced open, and he would not let himself drift off until he was exhausted past the point of resistance. He had come to believe that he was no longer the person he had been before. He felt like an object, not a person, as though the men who had held him had stripped away something essential and left only a shell. Worse, he believed that he had acted in ways that went against who he was—he had begged, he had cried, he had offered information about his company’s finances in exchange for promises of release. He was ashamed of this, and he told me that he felt he had betrayed himself. The people responsible had never been caught, and as far as he knew, they were still operating, still taking other hostages, still facing no consequences. This knowledge sat inside him like a stone.

The avoidance crept into every corner of his life. He stopped accepting invitations to social gatherings because he could not bear the casual physical affection that friends offered—a hand on the shoulder, a hug in greeting. Those touches made him flinch, and he was terrified that someone would notice and ask why. He also found that the sound of children crying, which he had never thought much about before, now made him feel nauseous and agitated. He had no children of his own, but he lived in a neighborhood with a playground, and he began leaving for work earlier and returning later to avoid passing by it. His divorce, which had happened the year after his return, was partly a consequence of this withdrawal. His wife had tried to understand, but he could not explain what was happening inside him, and eventually she had stopped trying. He had not dated since.

What brought him to my office was a moment two weeks ago. He had been in his apartment on a Sunday afternoon, the television on as usual, when the power went out. The sudden, absolute silence was so overwhelming that he found himself on the floor, his back against the wall, unable to move or speak for nearly an hour. When the power came back, he called his doctor the next morning. He told me he was afraid that he was losing his mind, but he was also afraid of what it might mean if he was not losing his mind—if this was simply how he was going to live now. He said he wanted to feel like a person again, but he was not sure that was possible.
